lesson.title: Current Sources on the Loop: Building a Supermesh
lesson.summary: A current source shared between two meshes has no defined voltage to sum in KVL, so a supermesh traces the combined outer boundary around both meshes and adds a constraint equation from the source's known current.
lesson.body:
A current source creates the same kind of trouble for the mesh current method that a voltage source creates for the node voltage method, just mirrored. KVL needs a voltage to sum around the loop, but a current source does not have a fixed voltage across it, its voltage depends entirely on the rest of the circuit. So when a current source sits in a branch shared by two meshes, with nothing else in series with it, you cannot write an ordinary KVL equation for either mesh individually. The fix mirrors the supernode trick exactly: merge the two meshes into a supermesh by drawing your KVL loop around the outer boundary of both meshes combined, skipping over the branch that contains the shared current source entirely.

This works because KVL only cares about the loop you actually trace, not about what other branches exist inside it. Tracing the combined outer boundary avoids the problematic current source branch altogether, giving you one honest KVL equation. That equation alone is not enough, since it now has two unknown mesh currents in it, so you add a second equation directly from the current source itself: since the source fixes the exact current through its branch, and that current is the difference of the two mesh currents flowing through it, you get a constraint equation for free, exactly parallel to the source constraint used in a supernode.

Consider this circuit: mesh 1, on the left, contains a 36 volt source and a 2 ohm resistor. Mesh 2, on the right, contains a 4 ohm resistor. The branch shared between them, instead of a resistor, contains a 3 amp current source oriented so that it forces I1 minus I2 to equal 3 amps, where both mesh currents are defined clockwise. The supermesh KVL equation, tracing the outer boundary and skipping the current source branch, is negative 36, plus I1 times 2, plus I2 times 4, equals zero, which simplifies to I1 plus 2I2 equals 18. The constraint from the source is I1 minus I2 equals 3, so I1 equals I2 plus 3.

Substituting, (I2 plus 3) plus 2I2 equals 18, so 3I2 equals 15, giving I2 equals 5 amps and I1 equals 8 amps. Check the constraint: 8 minus 5 is 3, correct. Check the supermesh equation directly: I1 times 2, plus I2 times 4, equals 8 times 2, plus 5 times 4, equals 16 plus 20, equals 36, matching the source exactly.

Supermeshes come up constantly in real circuits, since current sources, whether from transistor models or practical current source components, rarely happen to land in a branch by themselves shared with only one mesh. The pattern to remember is simple: whenever a current source blocks a clean KVL loop, stop trying to write two separate mesh equations and instead write one supermesh equation plus one constraint equation, the same two for one trade that a supernode makes on the node voltage side.
